summary: Ghana lies on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa; in 1957 it became the first country in sub-Saharan Africa to gain independence from colonial rule, and is known for political stability, gold and cocoa.

ranking.name: Pentecostal / Charismatic
ranking.description: Ghana's Pentecostal movement can be traced to the healing revival led in the 1920s by the local pastor Peter Anim; in 1937 the Irish missionary James McKeown came to Ghana and helped develop the Church of Pentecost, today the largest Protestant church. After the economic crisis of the 1980s and the democratization of the 1990s, large Charismatic churches stressing miraculous healing and prosperity theology rose rapidly in cities such as Accra and Kumasi, attracting large numbers of young people through television and radio, and making this the largest religious group in Ghana.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: From the 15th century Muslim merchants from Mali and the Hausa lands travelled south along the trans-Saharan trade routes to trade in northern kingdoms such as Dagbon and Gonja, and Islam was introduced with them. Muslims live mainly in the northern regions, and in southern cities there are also "Zongo" communities where Muslim migrants live together; Ghana's Muslims and Christians have long lived together peacefully.

ranking.name: Protestant Christianity
ranking.description: In the early 19th century European Protestant missions began evangelizing in the Gold Coast: the Swiss Basel Mission arrived in the Akuapem hills in 1828, the British Methodists set up a base at Cape Coast in 1835, and the German Bremen Mission preached among the Ewe in the east in 1847. They opened schools and translated the Bible, producing the first generation of Ghanaians with a Western education, and forming today's Presbyterian, Methodist and Evangelical Presbyterian churches.

ranking.name: Other Christian denominations
ranking.description: These include Seventh-day Adventists, Jehovah's Witnesses, and the African independent churches founded by local prophets and blending African traditional elements (such as the various "spiritual churches" that arose in the early 20th century), which have many followers in both rural areas and cities.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: The Portuguese brought Catholic priests as early as 1482 when they built the castle at Elmina, but real missionary work began in 1880 when priests of the Society of African Missions re-established the church at Elmina, and in the early 20th century the White Fathers entered the north to preach. Catholicism is known for its schools and hospitals, and has followers everywhere.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: The Akan believe in the supreme god Onyame, many spirits (abosom) and ancestors, and the Golden Stool of the Ashanti Kingdom is regarded as a symbol of the soul of the nation; the Ewe have the Vodu religion. Although very few people identify as following only a traditional religion, ancestor veneration, chiefly festivals and traditional rites are still widely woven into the lives of many Christians and Muslims.

religion.background: Ghana originally had the traditional beliefs of peoples such as the Akan, Ewe and Ga, while the north came into contact with Islam through the Saharan trade from the 15th century. At the end of the 15th century the Portuguese set up posts on the coast, and in the 19th century European Protestant and Catholic missions evangelized massively in the British-ruled Gold Coast and, through mission schools, shaped the modern elite. In 1957 Ghana became the first British colony in sub-Saharan Africa to gain independence, after which religious freedom developed, and in the late 20th century Pentecostalism and Charismatic Christianity grew explosively, making Ghana one of the most active Christian countries in Africa.

ranking.name: Akan (Twi, Fante)
ranking.description: Akan is the language of the Akan people of central and southern Ghana, and includes dialects such as Asante Twi, Akuapem Twi and Fante. The expansion of the Ashanti Empire, founded in 1701, spread Twi widely, and in the 19th century Johannes Christaller of the Basel Mission translated the Bible into Akuapem Twi and compiled a dictionary, laying down the written standard. Today Akan is the most widespread lingua franca in Ghana, and many non-Akan people can speak it.

ranking.name: Ewe
ranking.description: Ewe is spoken in the Volta Region in the east, and the Ewe moved from the city of Notsie in present-day Togo around the 17th century. In the colonial period the Ewe homeland was divided between the British Gold Coast and German Togo, and after World War I British Togoland joined Ghana by a referendum in 1956. The German Bremen Mission devised a written standard for Ewe in the 19th century.

language.history: Ghana has more than eighty languages, belonging mainly to the Kwa and Gur branches of the Niger–Congo family. Before colonization Akan became a regional lingua franca with the expansion of the Ashanti Empire, while the north was influenced by Hausa. In the 19th century European missionaries devised writing for Twi, Fante, Ewe and Ga and opened schools. British colonization made English the language of administration and education, and after independence in 1957 English was made the official language so as to cross ethnic lines; the government also promotes the teaching of more than ten Ghanaian languages in schools.

ranking.name: Jollof rice
ranking.description: Rice cooked in a red sauce of tomato, onion, chili and spices such as ginger and thyme, often served with fried chicken, beef or fried plantain.
ranking.history: The name jollof comes from the Jolof Empire of the Wolof people of the Senegambia region in the 14th–16th centuries, and the dish originates in the local tomato-and-fish rice, which later spread across West Africa with trade and migration. The Ghanaian version is often cooked with fragrant rice and differs in flavor from the Nigerian version, and the two countries' internet users have long had a playful argument known as the "Jollof Wars". In Ghana it is the indispensable star of parties such as birthdays, weddings and church gatherings.

ranking.name: Fufu
ranking.description: Boiled cassava and plantain are put into a wooden mortar and pounded repeatedly with a long pestle into an elastic dough, served with groundnut soup, palm nut soup or light soup.
ranking.history: Pounding starchy dough is an ancient West African food tradition, originally made with yam; in the 16th century the Portuguese introduced cassava from the Americas, and because of its high yield and drought tolerance it became the main ingredient of fufu. In Akan households the rhythm of fufu pounding, one person pounding and another turning the dough, is a familiar everyday sound and requires coordination and skill. Fufu is regarded as Ghana's most representative staple, and Sunday family lunch often features it with soup.

ranking.name: Banku
ranking.description: Fermented corn and cassava dough are mixed and stirred in a pot over heat into a smooth, slightly sour dough, often eaten with pepper sauce and grilled tilapia or okra soup.
ranking.history: Corn and cassava are both crops that the Portuguese introduced from the Americas to West Africa in the 16th century, and the coastal Ga and Ewe processed them by fermentation to make banku. Fermentation not only gives its characteristic sour taste but also lengthens storage time, which suits the tropical climate. Its pairing with grilled tilapia and pepper sauce is the signature of seaside restaurants in Accra, and it is also the everyday staple of people in coastal areas.

ranking.name: Waakye
ranking.description: Rice and beans cooked together with dried sorghum leaves added to give the rice a reddish-brown color, served with pepper sauce, spaghetti, boiled egg, fried fish and other toppings.
ranking.history: The name comes from the Hausa word "wake" (beans) of the north; it was originally the food of northern Muslim communities and became popular nationwide as northern migrants entered the southern cities. The coloring with sorghum leaves is its signature. Today waakye is Ghana's most popular street breakfast and lunch; roadside vendors wrap it in leaves, and customers can add various toppings as they like.

ranking.name: Kelewele (spicy fried plantain)
ranking.description: Ripe plantain is diced, marinated with ginger, chili, cloves and salt, and fried; it is crisp outside and sweet inside with some heat, and is often eaten as a snack with roasted peanuts.
ranking.history: Kelewele is the most common evening street snack in cities such as Accra, with vendors frying it fresh in large pans under the streetlights. Plantain has long been a main crop of southern Ghana, and seasoning it with ginger and chili reflects the West African taste for spicy, aromatic flavors. It is often regarded as a local snack of the Ga people, and with urbanization became a nationally popular snack, also often served as a side dish at parties.
